podcast.title: "I'll Be Home for Christmas" Copyright Controversy
podcast.body: Ram independently wrote "I'll Be Home for Christmas" in memory and registered its copyright in December 1942. He was shocked when Walter Kent and Kim Gannon released a strongly similar song, recorded by Bing Crosby, a few months later. His publishers, Mills Music, successfully sued to get Ram credited on future releases. "The story of Al Behon for Christmas was a rather controversial one."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Control of Five Platters Inc.
podcast.body: Book Ram was the controlling force behind "Five Platters Inc.," the corporation he established shortly after The Platters signed to Mercury, which held the rights to the band's name and was instrumental in the subsequent legal battles. "a corporation was up, five platters ink, which was controlled by Book Ram, and had all the members of the platters as shareholders."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Intent for Tony Williams' Solo Career
podcast.body: It appears that Book Ram's long-term plan, dating back to 1956, was to establish Tony Williams as a solo artist while simultaneously maintaining The Platters as a successful group, indicating a calculated management strategy for both entities. "Indeed, it seems they have been Book Ram's plan from the very start to get Williams to be a solo artist while keeping the platters as a hit group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Law Degree for Parents
podcast.body: Book Ram obtained a law degree, primarily to satisfy his parents' wishes, but his true passion remained songwriting. "He had obtained a law degree, mostly to please his parents."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Legitimate Songwriter Credibility
podcast.body: Unlike many managers of his era who took unearned songwriting credits, Book Ram was described as a songwriter of "great ability" who genuinely authored the Platters' songs he was credited for, with no suggestion that his credits were fraudulent. "there has never been any suggestion that Book VAM wasn't the sole author of the plotter's songs he's credited for."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Molding The Platters
podcast.body: Book Ram viewed The Platters as "material he could mold in his own image," indicating his desire for creative control and his intention to shape their sound and image to his specific vision. "he saw the platters as a means to that end, while material he could mold in his own image."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Narrative "Villain" Across Episodes
podcast.body: Book Ram is described as ending up being the "villain" in the narrative connecting the story of The Platters with that of The Penguins and "Earth Angel," suggesting his controversial management style and legal disputes positioned him negatively in the historical accounts. "BookVam ends up being the villain."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: New York Music Scene Involvement
podcast.body: In the late 1930s and early 1940s, Book Ram was significantly involved in the New York music scene, where he met Duke Ellington in an arranging class and was introduced by Ellington to prominent figures like Chick Webb, Cab Calloway, and Mills Music. "he seems to have been part of the music scene in New York, in the late 30s and early 40s in a big way."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Posthumous Impact on Name Rights
podcast.body: Book Ram had long been deceased by the time the legal disputes over The Platters' name were finally resolved in 2011, highlighting the enduring complexity of the legal structures he put in place. "By that point BookVam was long dead, as were all the members of the classic platters lineup except Herb Read."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Prolific Litigator
podcast.body: Book Ram was frequently involved in lawsuits, engaging in many legal battles with various individuals and entities throughout his career. "Book VAM would end up fighting a lot of lawsuits, with a lot of people."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Seven-Year Contract for The Platters
podcast.body: Upon signing The Platters, Book Ram secured a lengthy seven-year contract for the group, consisting of Tony Williams, Alex Hodge, David Lynch, and Herb Reed, reflecting his long-term plans for their development. "Ram signed the platters, now a four piece consisting of Williams, Alex Hodge, David Lynch and Herb Reed, to a seven-year contract."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Strategic Use of The Penguins
podcast.body: Book Ram managed The Penguins and secured their deal with Mercury Records only on the condition that The Platters were also signed. He then largely abandoned The Penguins, using their hit as leverage for his favored group. "But then the group got very lucky. Book Ram became the manager of the penguins... Ram agreed to the deal, but only on the condition that Mercury signed the platters as well."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Transition from Film Music to Management
podcast.body: Ram initially moved west with aspirations of breaking into the film music business but was unsuccessful. This inability to enter film scoring led him to transition into music management, though making music remained his primary passion. "made the mistake of moving west in order to get into the film music business, only to find that he couldn't break into the market and had to move into management instead."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
